text.content: MARSin the system. Their frontier culture was likened to the American Old West, with their saloons and dance halls to blow off steam, but the Martians were focused on their dream of making a new home for humanity. Mars’s lighter gravity caused changes to their physiology over the generations. Martians have lower muscle mass and bone density than Earthers, making them taller and more lithe-bodied, although not to the degree of Belters. Hormone treatments, blood oxygen boosters, muscle fatigue inhibi-tors, and bone density enhancers manage all of this and allow Martians to tolerate even Earth’s gravity, albeit with some emotional discomfort from the barely-disguised glee of Earthers at seeing proud Martians humbled.

Martians live their entire lives inside domed cities and tunnels under the surface, not experiencing the vastness of space the way Belters do. Generations spent in relatively close quarters means many Martians experience agoraphobia. The wide skies and seas of Earth leave many visiting Martians gasping and hyperventilating, panicking at the shocking openness. Martian visitors are often brought to Earth on the night side of the planet and told to focus only on the horizon when they step outside. Compared to Mars, the average Earth city is an overcrowded assault on every sensory and moral level; their home tunnels are clean and well-lit, and even with billions living in fairly close quarters, there’s a quiet to be found on Mars that is lost on Earth.

Modern Martian life expectancy exceeds 120 Earth-years; the oldest generation of Martians remember the days when the best Martian entertainment was fungal booze and an entertainment feed from Earth, which frequently issued directives and presumed to tell Mars what to do. The movement for independence is still within living memory as well, and it is this sense of entitlement and defiance that formed the bedrock and strata of Martian society. That generation of settlers built better ships, developed environmental science that outstripped Earth’s, and reached a degree of self-sufficiency previously thought impossible—and that was before a native Martian opened up the solar system with the Epstein Drive. For years, proud Mars looked back at an overcrowded Earth with a sense of pity. It was a world that had lost its way, where the vast majority of people lived indolently off the government dole, with nothing in their lives but meaningless entertainment, drugs, and sex. However, since witnessing the horrors of the Free Navy’s asteroid bombardment and the resulting casualties, Martian empathy for Earth has reawakened. Some who have remained on Mars have refocused their efforts, not just to the greening of the red planet, but to the healing of humanity’s wounded home world. Mars has a mere fraction of Earth’s population, even after the bombardment, as well as a fraction of Earth’s industrial base, but the Martian character is focused on hard-work and achievement. It also tends to manifest in a militaristic attitude and strong support for the Martian Navy and Marines. Until a generation or so ago, routine attack drills for schools were common, and three generations ago, the inevitable victory of Earth in a war hung like a dust storm over the whole of Mars. But things have changed. Many of the most militaristic Martians left with Duarte’s First Fleet, and Earth and Mars are now allies ostensibly, but the once-proud world that dared to defy Earth is a mere shadow of its former self. The vote of no-confidence that ousted former Prime Minister Nathan Smith after the Free Navy Conflict is a symbol of the blow that once unshakable Martian confidence has taken from recent events. Martian scientists discovered the protomolecule, kept it secret, and trusted corporate allies like Protogen to help them study and exploit it in the first place. Their belief in unity, following orders, and doing your part was exploited by Winston Duarte to effectively stage a silent coup behind everyone’s backs. Superior Martian military technology was handed to Belter terrorists, leading to a conflict that nearly destroyed Earth.

There is little Martians can do to atone for these crimes, but cutting-edge Martian environmental science is now devoted to cultivating colonies light years away, doing what it can to better all of On Mars, the joke went, a man’s humanity.

— “Drive”

Mars is a world of domes and vacuum-sealed, high-speed railways, shielded from a too-thin atmosphere and a too-harsh yet also too-distant Sun. It’s a world of spaceports, underground apartments (called “holes”), and massive hydroponic farms. Humanity dug deep into the soil and rock, crafting underground cities with UV sunlamps strung overhead, using the soil as insulation and radiation shielding in lieu of a planetary magnetosphere. The transparent ceramic insulation used by the earliest settlers to construct their walls and home-holes is starting to scratch and gray in the oldest settlements, the sealant warping and bubbling from the constant damp heat of humanity warring against the dry chill of Mars.

Life on Mars

Mars’s large population centers required a standardized language for military and government, and even today, many Martians default to English. Immigrants from Eastern and South Asia, the Americas, and other parts of Earth in the first and second generations led to a riotous variety of accents, maintained with characteristic Martian pride and equally characteristic stubbornness. It’s not unusual to meet a Martian with a strong Texan (especially from the Mariner Valley) or British English accent, no matter their ethnic heritage. Hydroponic farms grow crops in Martian soil, cultured from dirt and organisms drawn from Earth and naturally selected over hundreds of years—or otherwise meticulously crafted in planet-side laboratories. They’re fed melted water from deep under the surface or piped in from the polar ice caps, but this is a paltry harvest compared to hydration-rich Ganymede and Europa. Few Martians eat completely fresh food, the majority being potatoes, mushrooms, and varieties of coffee. Most eat meat grown in vats, along with varieties of vegetable paste resembling hummus. Their lasagnas are spread between layers of fake grains and smothered in fake tomato sauce and fake cheese, an evening’s repast to go with the morning’s breakfast of fake eggs. Martians visiting Earth, Ganymede, or Europa often take the opportunity to gorge. Real food still tends to be dehydrated and full of preservatives; despite this, Martians enjoy restaurants with some regularity, with a broad ethnic palate from a planet most have never seen: Thai hot pots, Italian pasta, Japanese ramen, and more. Sadly, many of those restaurants, cafés, and tea houses stand empty now, or they have been replaced by the old-style saloons and entertainment parlors, serving cheap liquor and equally cheap amusements.

Olympus Mons

The largest mountain in the Solar System is like a monument to Martian pride and ambition. Several cities, farms, and prisons with rock-breaking chain gangs cut deep into Olympus Mons. The most prominent is Hecate Base, the main training facility for the Martian Navy. The base has undergone renovation in recent years, but few things change in the massive steel facility visible from low orbit; sure, the crappy handball courts are gone and the Steel Cactus Mexican Grill is a Thai place now, but the complex still holds the pride of the Martian cadet corps. The slopes of Olympus Mons also host a dizzying array of towns and small cities. Syria Planum enjoys their closeness to Olympus, with a preponderance of Algerian and European immigrants leading to a long tradition of dense and complicated native Martian folk music going back generations.

The Mariner Valley

Valles Marineris stretches across the planet’s surface, a canyon beyond grand, four thousand kilometers of protection from the admittedly-gentle Martian elements. The Mariner Valley was settled by Chinese, East Indian, and Texan immigrants in one of the earliest waves of migration, and it remains one of the most well-developed areas of Mars. Sprawling across the sides of the canyons, five neighborhoods are linked by Haizhe, a network of bridges and tubes resembling nothing so much as a cartoon jellyfish. A high-speed rail line connects the Valley to Londres Nova. Spurred by their ancient heritage on Earth, the residents of the Mariner Valley maintain a cowboy attitude and manner of speech, leading to an affected plain spoken style and a propensity for drinking. It also led to a propensity for sports; football matches played in low Martian gravity are long-distance and graceful affairs, and the Mariner Valley teams enjoy a fanbase planet-wide.

Londres Nova

The city, such as it was, had burrowed deep into the flesh of Mars, using the soil as Londres Nova, “New London,” is a city in the northern reach of the Aurorae Sinus. Like most Martian cities, it’s a partly-underground webwork of tunnels, dotted with tube insulation and radiation shielding with only ten stations determining the social structure of the long since built-up residential areas. domes pressing out into the surface. Ten agricultural domes press out to the surface, and seven neighborhoods radiate out —Gods of Riskbelow. The oldest parts of the city bear the early marks of colonization, scars carved into the planet by automated construction robots and the preference of the earliest colonists for function over form.

Londres Nova’s two former industrial neighborhoods, Nariman and Martineztown, are struggling to reinvent themselves, with mostly lower-class families living there. The worst parts of town are Innis Deep and Innis Shallows, each has only a single tube route, making them cul-de-sacs and havens for Belter-like Martians—antisocial and fiercely inde - pendent. Drug dealers prowl the underbelly of the city, recruiting young chemists from the university to cook high-quality narcotics for sale to the Martian population. Despite this, they’re perhaps the most welcoming of outsiders (if only because outsiders can’t get an apartment anywhere else). Martians involved in social outreach frequently move there to help the dispossessed.

Dhanbad Nova

The research center at Dhanbad Nova, host to a wide variety of government-funded initiatives and regional research wings, remains one of the largest on Mars. The anti-cancer regimens available aboard every Martian ship were developed here, as well as the most commonly utilized water reclamation techniques. Today, Dhanbad Nova is still a hub of research, but it now has the standard complement of Martian hotels with all the supposed decadence of an Earther: fancy soaps, large baths, fluffy towels—the works. Visitors to the research facilities can enjoy all the luxuries of home, no matter from where they hail—and they hail from everywhere. Powerful conglomerates such as Masstech and interplanetary concerns such as Kwikowski Mutual Interest Group maintain large stakes in the laboratories of Dhanbad Nova. Their corporate structures occupy massive levels both above and below the surface, between the noodle bars and the other evidence of ancient colonization,

In contrast to the bloated bureaucracy and centuries-old grudges of the UN, the Martian Congressional Republic is organized and efficient, driven by a united political will, or so they thought. This unity and drive made Mars a worthy rival to Earth, despite the former’s smaller population. Whether or not Mars could have truly outstripped and overcome Earth remains a largely academic question at this point, as the two allied worlds both struggle to deal with their current challenges. The MCR has a parliamentary government built from the ground-up rather than the UN’s somewhat ad hoc development on Earth. Although Martians do not have a much higher opinion of politicians than Earthers, government service is still considered a civic duty on Mars. For the longest time, Martians tended to favor politicians who embodied their world’s pioneering spirit. Support for the Great Endeavor and the Martian military—and a willingness to trash-talk Earth—were the key qualities for elect-ability. The MCR spends a substantial amount on military research and development, ensuring their ships are on the cutting-edge, and military R&D often found its way back into civilian applications. Many companies retain concerns on Mars, and corporate citizens are common there. Nowadays, both Earth and Mars maintain research stations on various moons and parts of the system and cooperate in joint projects, such as research into space elevators for both planets.

For nearly all of its history, the Martian Congressional Republic Navy (MCRN) has known the threat of war, and it has trained and prepared itself accordingly. The past generation of Martian military has seen more front-line action than all of the previous generations combined: the loss of the Donnager, the Ganymede incident, the conflict near Io, the Ring and the Slow Zone, and the Free Navy Conflict. What’s worse, the MCRN has known betrayal of the worst kind. Winston Duarte and his allies absconded with a full third of the Martian fleet and over ten thousand personnel, leaving the once proud Martian Navy and Marines weakened and demoralized. Combine that with losses during the Free Navy Conflict and Mars is no longer quite the military force it once was.

Design & Deployment

Most Martian ships contain the same rough format: floor by floor from the drive cone and reactors, layered on layer with engineering deck, specialty compartments, galley and crew cabins, medical bays and interrogation chambers, storage deck and airlocks, then the command deck and pilot farthest forward (or the bridge in larger ships). Under thrust, Martian ships are skyscrapers, with ladders between hatches leading between decks. MCRN ships cruise separately from one another, or in the case of smaller ships, in tight pairs. The third-generation battleships are mobile fleets unto themselves. The pride of the MCRN is the Donnager-class dreadnought, named after the former flagship, lost to Protogen’s stealth ships at the start of the incident with the Protomolecule. Donnager dreadnoughts measure nearly 500 meters in length, about that of a 130-story office building, and bristle with torpedo tubes, point defense cannons, and rail guns. They are large enough to carry smaller missile frigates or escort corvettes within them. Second-generation battleships still serve a place in the navies, alongside fast-attack cruisers, destroyers, frigates, and corvettes capable of patrolling the entire Solar system. Mars also has advanced stealth technology, though dreadnoughts and larger ships typically eschew this in favor of an aggressive posture designed to intimidate. Larger ships are bases unto themselves, carrying marines and military interrogators aided by pharmaceuticals—focus drugs to make sure they don’t miss the smallest detail. The exploratory and military arms of Mars are the finest ships in the system, barring exotic flagships funded by the ultra-wealthy of Earth. Pound for pound, any Martian ship can defeat an equivalent Earth or Belter craft by virtue of superior technology, fiercer armament, and better-trained crew. Martians never cease to remind others of this fact and let their pride show at the slightest opportunity.

The Martian Marine Corps

The Martian Martine Corps (MMC) is the field infantry branch of the MCRN, serving on Martian ships, stations, and outposts throughout the system. The MMC is divided into Infantry, Armor, and Force Recon divisions, with Infantry making use of Martian light armor, Armor units using massive combat mechs like the Yojimbo, four meters tall and equipped with heavy weapons. Force Recon are Martian Special Forces and use Goliath-class power armor suits in the field. Martian Marines are known for their training, grit, and determination. Although they benefit from cutting-edge technology, it’s their esprit de corps and devotion to duty that sets them most apart.

10: The Belt & the Outers ccording to the United Nations, fifty million people live in the rocks and habitats beyond Earth and Mars. Ask the people who actually live there and they’ll say the number edges up closer to a hundred million. The inhabitants of the Belt— beltalowda to themselves, Belters to the inyalowda of the Inner Planets—were the dispossessed and forgotten of those who came from Earth. Marked by a sense of self-reliance in the face of an obvious lack of self-sufficiency, and quiet resilience, the Belter psyche endures as a powerful force in the System, particularly in the Transport Union era. Out beyond the asteroid belt itself, in the shadow of the vast gas giants, Belters maintained an existence dedicated to fueling the ambitions of others. They were often styled as colonists, but unlike the hopes of Martians, nobody believed the Belt would ever become more habitable than it already was. Air finds no purchase here, crops do not grow in solid rock, and few natural resources exist to support life. Those working the asteroid belt harvest minerals and send massive haulers to break great, icy asteroids apart for water. Earth and Mars became dependent on the mineral and scientific wealth of the Belt to maintain their standards of living, but they gave little in return. Prior to the Eros incident, much of the Belt was technically a United Nations protectorate governed by Earth—though one living under constant fear of seizure by Mars. Earth would naturally launch a full-scale war in retaliation, leaving the Belt to lose no matter who won in the end. The Outer Planets Alliance (OPA) tried to give voice to the needs of the Belters, often using the only tool of the oppressed and unheard: violent protest. Eventually, the Free Navy, a faction of the OPA, armed with weapons and resources from a breakaway Martian faction, visited that violence on Earth, Mars, and the rest of the System. In the wake of that conflict, and the negotiations to bring peace, the Belters have taken their place as the people who truly understand the expanse between the planets and stars in the form of the Transport Union.

The earliest Belters were miners, living out of ships and sustaining themselves on years’ worth of food reserves. It wasn’t until the Epstein Drive that the Belt truly opened to humanity, allowing life and culture to flourish. Humans have been among the asteroids for a shorter amount of time than they have been on Mars, but more than a century of living in microgravity has led to physical changes in Belters. Eros and Ceres were spun up to generate their own gravity, but this is a poor substitute
